items.stem: The diagram shows three levers. F is the fulcrum, L is the load, and E is where the effort is applied. Which lever is a second-class lever?
choices: All three are the same class
items.explanation: A lever's class is set by what sits in the middle. In a first-class lever the fulcrum is in the middle (A, like a seesaw). In a second-class lever the load is in the middle (B, like a wheelbarrow). In a third-class lever the effort is in the middle (C, like a broom or tweezers).

items.stem: The lever in the diagram rests on a fulcrum. A 120 lb load sits 2 ft from the fulcrum and the effort is applied 6 ft from the fulcrum on the other side. Ignoring the weight of the bar, what effort is needed to balance the load?
items.explanation: Balance means effort x effort arm = load x load arm: E x 6 = 120 x 2 = 240, so E = 40 lb. The mechanical advantage is 6/2 = 3, and 120/3 = 40. Multiplying 120 x 2 x 1.5 or dividing 120 by 2 gives the wrong distractors.

items.stem: Which of these tools is a third-class lever, with the effort applied between the fulcrum and the load?
choices: A claw hammer pulling a nail
items.explanation: Tweezers pivot where the two arms join, you squeeze in the middle, and the load is at the tips, so the effort is between the fulcrum and the load. A wheelbarrow is second class (load in the middle). A seesaw and a claw hammer are first class (fulcrum in the middle).

items.stem: The block and tackle in the diagram lifts a 200 lb load. The upper block is fixed to the ceiling and the lower block moves with the load. Ignoring friction and the weight of the blocks, about how much pull is needed on the free end of the rope?
items.explanation: Count the rope segments that support the moving block: four. Each carries one quarter of the load, so the pull is 200/4 = 50 lb. Counting the two pulleys instead of the four rope segments gives 100 lb, which is wrong. The trade-off is that you must pull 4 ft of rope for every 1 ft the load rises.

items.stem: In the diagram, pulley A is fixed to the ceiling and pulley B is a movable pulley that rises with its load. Each supports a 100 lb weight. Ignoring friction, which statement is correct?
choices: A needs about 100 lb of pull and B needs about 50 lb
A needs about 50 lb of pull and B needs about 100 lb
Both need about 100 lb of pull
Both need about 50 lb of pull
items.explanation: A single fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull, so the force is still 100 lb. A movable pulley is held up by two rope segments, so each carries 50 lb and the pull is 50 lb (but you pull twice as much rope).

items.stem: A 400 lb barrel is pushed up the ramp in the diagram. The ramp is 12 ft long along the slope and rises 3 ft. Ignoring friction, what force is needed to push the barrel up the ramp?
items.explanation: The ideal mechanical advantage of a ramp is length divided by height: 12/3 = 4. The needed force is 400/4 = 100 lb. Dividing the weight by the height alone (400/3) or multiplying by the ratio (400 x 4) are common errors.

items.stem: Two steel wedges have the same length, but one is thinner at the back than the other. Compared with the thicker wedge, the thinner wedge driven into a log
choices: needs less force per blow but must be driven farther to open the same gap
needs more force per blow but splits the log in fewer blows
produces the same splitting force from the same blow
items.explanation: A wedge is a moving inclined plane. Its mechanical advantage is length divided by thickness, so a thinner wedge of the same length has a larger mechanical advantage and multiplies the hammer blow more. The price is distance: it must travel farther into the log to spread the wood the same amount.

items.stem: A bolt has 16 threads per inch. How many complete turns of the nut move it 3/4 inch along the bolt?
items.explanation: Each full turn moves the nut one thread pitch, which is 1/16 inch. To move 3/4 inch takes (3/4) / (1/16) = (3/4) x 16 = 12 turns. The fine pitch is why a screw is such a strong force multiplier: many turns for a small advance.

items.stem: The windlass in the diagram has a wheel of radius 12 in on the same shaft as an axle of radius 3 in. A 30 lb pull on a rope wrapped around the wheel lifts a load on a rope wrapped around the axle. Ignoring friction, what is the largest load it can lift?
items.explanation: A wheel and axle is a lever that turns: effort x wheel radius = load x axle radius. 30 x 12 = load x 3, so load = 360/3 = 120 lb. The mechanical advantage is 12/3 = 4. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 7.5 lb.

items.stem: Three gears A, B, and C mesh in a row as shown, and gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear C turn?
choices: Clockwise only if B has more teeth than A
Counterclockwise only if B has more teeth than A
items.explanation: Every pair of meshing gears turns in opposite directions. A clockwise makes B counterclockwise, and B counterclockwise makes C clockwise. The middle gear is an idler: its size changes nothing about direction or the speed ratio between A and C.

items.stem: Gear A drives gear B in the diagram. Using the tooth counts shown, how many complete turns does gear B make while gear A makes 9 turns?
items.explanation: Meshing teeth pass one for one, so turns of A x teeth of A = turns of B x teeth of B. 9 x 12 = 108 teeth pass, and 108/36 = 3 turns of B. The larger gear always turns slower. Multiplying 9 by the 3 to 1 ratio instead of dividing gives 27.

items.stem: In the compound gear train shown, gear A drives gear B. Gear C is fixed to the same shaft as B, so it turns with B, and C drives gear D. Using the tooth counts shown, if A turns at 600 rpm, how fast does D turn?
items.explanation: Work one stage at a time. A to B: 600 x 8/24 = 200 rpm, and C turns at 200 rpm because it shares B's shaft. C to D: 200 x 12/24 = 100 rpm. Stopping after the first stage gives 200 rpm, and B and D having the same tooth count does not make them turn at the same speed.

items.stem: Pulley A is driven clockwise as shown. An open belt connects A to B, and a crossed belt connects B to C. Which way does pulley C turn?
choices: The same way as B only if B and C are the same size
It cannot turn because the belt is crossed
items.explanation: An open belt makes both pulleys turn the same way, so B turns clockwise like A. A crossed belt reverses direction, so C turns counterclockwise. Pulley size changes speed, never direction.

items.stem: A 4-inch pulley on a motor shaft turns at 900 rpm and drives a 12-inch pulley with a belt. How fast does the 12-inch pulley turn?
items.explanation: The belt moves at the same speed over both pulleys, so rpm x diameter is the same for each: 900 x 4 = rpm x 12, giving 300 rpm. The larger pulley turns slower; 2,700 rpm is what you get by multiplying instead of dividing.

items.stem: In a power drill, a small plastic gear meshes with a steel gear. The drill bit jams solid while the motor keeps trying to turn. What is most likely to happen?
choices: The teeth of the plastic gear strip, because plastic is weaker than steel and the teeth carry the full motor torque
The teeth of the steel gear strip first, because the larger gear carries more force
Both gears strip equally, because meshing teeth always share damage equally
Nothing is damaged, because a jam removes the force from the gear teeth
items.explanation: Meshing teeth push on each other with the same force, so the weaker material fails first. A jam is the worst case: the motor's full torque is stopped at the teeth instead of being spent turning the bit. Plastic gears are often used on purpose as a cheap part that fails before the expensive parts do.

items.stem: A worker lifts a 40 lb box straight up onto a shelf 5 ft above the floor. How much work is done on the box?
items.explanation: Work equals force times the distance moved in the direction of the force: 40 lb x 5 ft = 200 ft-lb. Adding (45) or dividing (8) the numbers is not work. Carrying the box sideways at the same height would do no work against gravity.

items.stem: A hoist raises a 1,100 lb engine 20 ft in 40 seconds. One horsepower equals 550 ft-lb per second. What power is the hoist delivering?
items.explanation: Work = 1,100 x 20 = 22,000 ft-lb. Power = work / time = 22,000 / 40 = 550 ft-lb per second, which is exactly 1 hp. Forgetting to divide by the time gives 40 hp; dividing by 20 instead of 40 gives 2 hp.

items.stem: A 20 lb rock rests on a ledge 10 ft above the ground, so it has 200 ft-lb of potential energy. It falls off. Ignoring air resistance, how much kinetic energy does it have when it is 4 ft above the ground?
items.explanation: Total energy stays at 200 ft-lb. At 4 ft the remaining potential energy is 20 x 4 = 80 ft-lb, so the kinetic energy is 200 - 80 = 120 ft-lb. The 80 ft-lb answer is the potential energy, not the kinetic energy; energy is never added (280) during a free fall.

items.stem: A mechanic uses a jack to raise a 1,500 lb car 6 inches. To do it, he pushes the handle with 60 lb of force through a total handle travel of 25 ft. What is the efficiency of the jack?
items.explanation: Convert to matching units first: 6 inches is 0.5 ft. Work out = 1,500 x 0.5 = 750 ft-lb. Work in = 60 x 25 = 1,500 ft-lb. Efficiency = 750/1,500 = 50%. The missing half is lost to friction in the jack. No real machine reaches 100%.

items.stem: Two people push on the crate in the diagram. One pushes it to the right with 50 lb and the other pushes it to the left with 20 lb. Ignoring friction, what is the net force on the crate?
items.explanation: Forces in opposite directions subtract: 50 - 20 = 30 lb, in the direction of the larger force (right). Forces add to 70 lb only when they act in the same direction, and they cancel only when they are equal.

items.stem: A 60 lb child sits 4 ft from the center of the seesaw in the diagram. How far from the center must an 80 lb child sit on the other side to balance it?
items.explanation: Balance the torques (weight x distance) on each side: 60 x 4 = 240, so 80 x d = 240 and d = 3 ft. The heavier child sits closer to the center. Dividing the other way (80 x 4 / 60) gives about 5.3 ft, which would make the seesaw tip toward the heavier child.

items.stem: A light 12 ft beam rests on post A and post B at its ends. A 300 lb load is placed 3 ft from post A, as shown. How much of the load does post B carry?
items.explanation: Take moments about post A. The load's moment is 300 x 3 = 900 ft-lb, and post B's upward force balances it at 12 ft: B x 12 = 900, so B = 75 lb. Post A carries the rest, 225 lb. The post closer to the load carries more; 150 lb would be right only if the load were centered.

items.stem: Wrenches A and B in the diagram fit the same nut. A is 6 in long and B is 12 in long, and the same 20 lb force is applied at the end of each handle. Compared with wrench A, how much torque does wrench B put on the nut?
items.explanation: Torque = force x distance from the pivot. A gives 20 x 6 = 120 in-lb and B gives 20 x 12 = 240 in-lb, so B gives twice the torque. This is why wrenches and breaker bars are made long: the same hand force turns a tighter nut.

items.stem: On the balanced beam in the diagram, a 40 lb weight sits 2 ft to the left of the fulcrum and a 20 lb weight sits 5 ft to the left. A single weight 6 ft to the right balances them. How much does it weigh?
items.explanation: Add the left-side torques: 40 x 2 + 20 x 5 = 80 + 100 = 180 ft-lb. The right side must match: W x 6 = 180, so W = 30 lb. Simply adding the weights (60 lb) ignores the distances.

items.stem: The tank in the diagram is full of water and has three small holes, A, B, and C, in its side. From which hole does water leave with the greatest pressure?
choices: The pressure is the same at all three
items.explanation: Water pressure increases with depth because of the weight of the water above. Hole C is deepest, so its pressure and exit speed are greatest. The shape or width of the tank does not matter, only the depth below the surface.

items.stem: In the hydraulic press shown, a 40 lb force pushes down on the small piston, which has an area of 2 sq in. The large piston has an area of 20 sq in. What force does the large piston push up with?
items.explanation: The pressure in the fluid is 40 lb / 2 sq in = 20 psi, and Pascal's principle says it is the same everywhere in the fluid. On 20 sq in that pressure produces 20 x 20 = 400 lb. The force multiplies by the area ratio 20/2 = 10. Dividing instead gives 4 lb.

items.stem: The pump piston of a hydraulic jack has an area of 1 sq in and the lift piston has an area of 25 sq in. Each pump stroke pushes the small piston down 5 inches. How far does the lift piston rise on each stroke?
items.explanation: The fluid is not compressed, so the volume pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume entering the large one: 1 x 5 = 25 x d, so d = 5/25 = 0.2 in. The jack multiplies force 25 times but divides distance by 25, which is why you pump many times to raise a car a few inches.

items.stem: According to Pascal's principle, when pressure is applied to a confined fluid, the pressure
choices: is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls
is greatest near the point where it is applied and fades with distance
acts only in the direction of the applied force
is lost as the fluid is squeezed into a smaller volume
items.explanation: A confined liquid passes pressure on equally in all directions without loss. That is what lets a hydraulic brake pedal push on all four wheel cylinders at once with the same pressure. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so they do not absorb the pressure.

items.stem: Containers A, B, and C in the diagram have different shapes but are filled with water to the same depth of 10 inches. In which container is the water pressure on the bottom greatest?
choices: The pressure is the same in all three
items.explanation: Pressure at a depth depends only on the depth and the liquid, not on the shape or width of the container or how much water it holds. All three bottoms are 10 inches below the surface, so the pressure is equal. The total force on each bottom differs because the bottom areas differ, but the question asks about pressure.

items.stem: A metal casting weighs 30 lb on a scale in air. When it hangs from the scale fully underwater, it pushes aside water that weighs 4 lb. What does the scale read underwater?
items.explanation: Archimedes' principle: the water pushes up on the casting with a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces, 4 lb. The scale reads 30 - 4 = 26 lb. The casting sinks because it weighs more than the water it displaces, but it still feels lighter.

items.stem: The diagram shows a siphon draining the tank into a bucket. A is the end of the tube under the water, B is the top of the tube, and C is the outlet. Once the tube is full of water, it keeps flowing as long as
choices: C stays below the water surface in the tank and the tube stays full of water
B stays below the water surface in the tank
A is at exactly the same height as C
the bucket is raised higher than the tank
items.explanation: A siphon is driven by the height difference between the water surface in the tank and the outlet C. Water in the long leg falls and pulls water over the top behind it. The top B must be above the surface (that is how it gets over the rim), and if air enters the tube or C rises above the surface the flow stops.

items.stem: A coil spring is 6 inches long with nothing hanging from it and 8 inches long with a 10 lb weight hanging from it. Within its elastic limit, how long will it be with a 25 lb weight hanging from it?
items.explanation: Hooke's law: stretch is proportional to load. 10 lb stretches the spring 2 inches, so 25 lb stretches it 2 x 2.5 = 5 inches, and the length is 6 + 5 = 11 inches. Scaling the whole loaded length (8 x 2.5 = 20) is the common mistake; only the stretch scales, not the spring's free length.

items.stem: Two identical springs hold the same weight W in two ways, as shown. In A the springs hang side by side from the ceiling and share the weight. In B they hang end to end. If the weight in A drops 1 inch when it is hung, how far does the weight in B drop?
items.explanation: In A each spring carries half of W and stretches 1 inch, so a single spring under the full W would stretch 2 inches. In B each spring carries the full W, so each stretches 2 inches and the stretches add: 4 inches. Springs side by side are stiffer; springs end to end are softer.

items.stem: The block in the diagram is sliding down the ramp. Which arrow shows the direction of the friction force acting on the block?
items.explanation: Sliding friction always acts along the surface, opposite to the direction of motion. The block moves down the slope, so friction points up the slope (A). B is the direction of motion, C is the direction the block presses into the ramp, and D is the pull of gravity.

items.stem: A heavy wooden crate is dragged across a concrete floor at a steady speed, first resting on its large bottom face and then tipped onto one of its narrow sides. The force needed to keep it sliding
choices: is about the same either way, because sliding friction depends on the weight and the surfaces, not the contact area
is less on the narrow side, because less wood touches the floor
is greater on the narrow side, because the crate presses harder on each square inch
is less on the large face, because the weight is spread out
items.explanation: For dry sliding, friction = coefficient x normal force. Tipping the crate does not change its weight or the two materials, so the friction is about the same. A smaller area does press harder per square inch, but on fewer square inches, and the two effects cancel.

items.stem: Blocks A, B, C, and D in the diagram are made of the same solid material. The dot marks each block's center of gravity. Which block is hardest to tip over?
items.explanation: An object tips when its center of gravity moves past the edge of its base. A wide base and a low center of gravity both make that harder, and D has both. A, tall and narrow, tips most easily. B is wide but tall; C is low but narrow.

items.stem: A forklift operator drives across the warehouse with the load raised high instead of just above the floor. What is the main danger?
choices: The center of gravity of the forklift and load is higher, so it tips more easily on turns and bumps
The load weighs more when it is higher off the ground
The forks lose their mechanical advantage at full height
More weight shifts to the rear wheels, making the steering too light
items.explanation: Raising the load raises the combined center of gravity, so a smaller tilt or a sharp turn moves it outside the wheelbase and the truck tips. The weight itself does not change with height. Loads are carried low for the same reason a sailboat has a heavy keel and a crane keeps its boom low when traveling.

items.stem: Each rectangular frame in the diagram is made of boards joined by single nails at the corners, so the joints can pivot. Which frame cannot be pushed sideways into a leaning parallelogram shape?
items.explanation: A rectangle with pinned corners can rack (lean), but a triangle cannot change shape without changing the length of a side. The diagonal in B splits the rectangle into two triangles and locks it. The horizontal bar in C and the vertical bar in D just make more rectangles, which still rack.

items.stem: A load pushes down on the peak of the simple triangular truss in the diagram. The two ends rest on supports, and the right support is a roller that can slide. Which members are in tension (being stretched)?
choices: None, all three are in compression
items.explanation: The load pushes down the two sloping members A and B, squeezing them (compression). Their lower ends push outward and would spread apart, but the bottom member C ties the two feet together, so C is pulled from both ends (tension). This is why the bottom chord of a roof truss is called a tie.

items.stem: A thermostat uses a strip made of a layer of brass bonded to a layer of steel. Brass expands more than steel when heated. When the strip is heated, it
choices: bends toward the steel side, because the brass becomes the longer, outer side of the curve
bends toward the brass side, because brass expands more
bends toward whichever side is heated first
items.explanation: Both layers are bonded, so they must stay the same length at the joint even though the brass wants to be longer. The strip curves with the longer brass on the outside and the shorter steel on the inside, so it bends toward the steel. The movement opens or closes an electrical contact.
